description: Hola, soy José Correa. Estudiante de ingeniería de software enfocado en dar soluciones desde otra perspectiva más creativa y por lo general, fuera de lo común. Busco integrantes con intereses competitivos y conocimientos pero, sobre todo ganas de aprender de los demás.
summary: LIGHTMINUTE is a health-monitoring and decision-support prototype for astronauts on long missions, built for the “Health Monitoring for Astronauts” challenge. When Earth is 20 light-minutes away, the crew cannot wait for a flight surgeon to interpret a trend, and with a crew of four, population averages are not a meaningful reference. LIGHTMINUTE learns each astronaut’s own baseline with a per-person Bayesian (N-of-1) engine, fuses several weak signals that shift together, and adds hazards such as space weather and cabin CO₂ as context without letting them raise an alarm alone. It shows three lenses side by side (Earth rule, space-adapted rule, personal baseline), so it can flag a heart rate that is normal for the population but unusual for that astronaut. A deterministic engine decides; an optional LLM only explains, behind a verifier, so the system keeps working without the model or the link. The crew gets cited Decision Cards: what changed, what to do now, when to escalate, and what to tell Earth. Prototype on synthetic crews and public NASA/NOAA data; not a medical device.
details:
What it does: LIGHTMINUTE monitors six indicators per astronaut (resting heart rate, temperature, sleep, PVT reaction time, cabin CO₂, headache score) and turns them into cited Decision Cards with a level: info, watch, act or escalate. A crew tablet (Glance → Why → Act), a ground console with a light-delay message queue, and a step-by-step protocol runner present the result.

How it works: Quality control removes impossible readings. A per-person Bayesian baseline (Normal-Inverse-Gamma with Student-t predictive) learns each astronaut’s own normal, and a directional syndrome score fuses weak signals that move together. Space weather and cabin CO₂ add context but never raise an alarm alone. A deterministic engine sets numbers and urgency; an optional LLM only writes the explanation, and a verifier rejects invented citations or numbers, diagnosis wording and doses. If it rejects twice, a deterministic template card is shown.

Benefits and expected impact: It works with a crew of four, where population averages do not exist; it surfaces changes hidden inside the “normal range” (day 16 of the demo: a resting HR of 68.5 bpm is normal for the population but unusual for that astronaut); and it keeps working when the model, the link, or both are gone. We hope it helps crews on delayed-communication missions decide what to re-measure, when to escalate and what to tell Earth.

Results (synthetic benchmark, equal false-alarm budget): the directional N-of-1 syndrome detector recovered 71% / 96% / 100% of mild / moderate / strong shifts, versus 18% / 38% / 91% for a population threshold. On a heterogeneous crew: 66% / 93% / 100% versus 9% / 13% / 27%.

What is creative: three lenses side by side with named disagreement patterns; an LLM that explains but cannot decide, behind a verifier; light-delay-aware routing; and we published a calibration defect we found in our own model and how we fixed it.

Factors we considered: no diagnosis and no doses (decision support for trained crew, not a medical device); every claim cited or marked unverified; every data source labelled synthetic, proxy or real-public; consent tiers before anything is stored; a tamper-evident SHA-256 audit chain; offline operation.

Tools: Python 3.11, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI, Pydantic; React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js (3D anatomy); a TypeScript physiology simulator; Pyodide for a local offline engine; SubtleCrypto and Ed25519 signatures; GitHub Actions CI; optional DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Software only, no special hardware.

Known limits: the data are synthetic crews plus public datasets, not clinical validation. The LLM path was tested with a simulated client and not against the live API. On real heart-rate data (MMASH proxy) the interval coverage is 66.37%, below our 90–98% target; we document it as a blocker in the model card. Mild scenarios are deliberately weak.
